edges.description: Impaired cholinergic intestinal motility produces constipation, classically the first sign.

Abrupt respiratory failure can present as sudden unexpected death; a minority of C. botulinum isolates in a large archive came from sudden-death infants.

nodes.description: Serial respiratory and feeding monitoring, airway protection, mechanical ventilation when required, and nutritional support sustain the infant while neuromuscular transmission recovers. Aminoglycoside and other neuromuscular-blocking antibiotics should be avoided because they can worsen the paralysis.

nodes.description: BIG-IV (BabyBIG) is the first-line, form-specific antitoxin for infant intestinal botulism caused by toxin type A or B. It is human-derived rather than equine, and prompt administration shortens hospital, intensive-care, ventilation, and feeding-support duration. It neutralizes circulating toxin but cannot reverse paralysis already established within neurons.

nodes.description: Absorbed toxin binds peripheral cholinergic terminals, is internalized, and its light-chain metalloprotease cleaves SNARE proteins, preventing acetylcholine exocytosis at somatic motor and autonomic cholinergic terminals. This presynaptic functional denervation underlies both the motor and the autonomic features of infant botulism.
